that’s fair phrase

also that’s not fair, not fair!, it’s not fair, I think that’s fair, that’s not fair of you, unfair

classical

Plaut. Bacch. 1.2.11: tū dīs nec rēctē dīcis: nōn aequum facis (Lewis & Short), s.v. neque
Traupman 98
Traupman 312

Nōn aequum facis.

aequum, neuter of aequus, as the object of facere: “you are not doing what is fair”

that’s not fair of you

Other words

  • Id aequī faciō. — I accept it, I’m content with it

    aequī, genitive of value, with facere: “I count it as fair” · also used · classical · Ter. Heaut. 4.5.40: istuc aequī bonīque faciō (Lewis & Short s.v. aequus); Plaut. Mil. 3.1.189: aequī istuc faciam, it will be all the same to me (Lewis & Short); Traupman 98; Traupman 312

    Traupman gives it for “I think that’s fair”. Lewis & Short renders aequī bonīque facere “to regard as fair and reasonable, to put up with, be content with, acquiesce in”, and its examples are all of accepting what one cannot change: it answers “I’m content with it, it’s all the same to me” (see it makes no difference) better than a judgement that something is fair.

See also reasonable, it makes no difference.

SourcesLewis & Short: aequus

John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, pp. 98, 312.

Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, in the house spelling; they have not been checked against a modern edition.
